opus-5.5.text:
Oh, I really like it. It's not a fancy place at all, and I think that's kind of the point. When you walk in, the first thing you notice is that it doesn't feel like a typical tech office. There are robots everywhere. You'll see arms set up on tables, people teleoperating, collecting data, someone folding laundry with a robot in one corner and someone else debugging a policy in another. It's a little messy, honestly, but in a good way. It feels like a workshop more than an office.

What I appreciate most is how close everything is. The people training the models and the people running the robots are sitting a few meters apart. If I train a new checkpoint, I can literally walk over and watch it run on a real robot within the same afternoon. That tight loop between the model and the physical world is really important for this kind of research. You can read evaluation numbers all day, but watching a robot actually try to do a task tells you things the numbers don't.

It also shapes the culture. Because everything is so visible, people just wander over and ask, "Hey, what's going on with this one?" or "Why did it fail there?" A lot of good ideas come out of those casual conversations. There isn't much hierarchy in the space, either. Very senior researchers are right there next to the robots, getting their hands dirty like everyone else.

So, it's not glamorous, but for doing robotics research I think it's close to ideal. It feels like a place where things are being built, and that's very energizing to be around every day.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I love it. It's this old building in San Francisco, and the thing people notice first is that it doesn't feel like a typical AI lab at all. It feels more like a workshop. You walk in and there are robots everywhere, half-assembled arms on tables, laundry baskets, kitchen setups with dishes in the sink, because that's literally where we're collecting data and running evaluations.

What I like most is that there's no separation between the people writing the code and the physical world the robots have to work in. If a policy fails, you don't look at a log, you walk ten meters and watch the robot fail in front of you. That changes how you think about the problem. You stop treating it as an abstract benchmark and start noticing things like, oh, the lighting changed at four in the afternoon, or the towel is a different texture today.

It's also a little chaotic. It's loud, there's always something moving, and the data collection team is constantly rearranging scenes. But I think that's the right environment for this kind of work. Robotics is messy, and the office being messy in the same way keeps everyone honest about what the real problem actually is.
